topic: Why does time slow down when you move faster?
audience: Curious adult who recognizes clocks but expects one universal elapsed time
objective: Explain why Earth assigns more time to the same half-tick than the ship does.
takeaway: Same events, same light speed, longer path in Earth's frame.
prior: A clock can be imagined as one light pulse bouncing between two mirrors.
misconceptions: Earth sees the pulse hit the mirror at its OLD position
The viewpoints measure different light speeds
The two diagrams depict different pulses
The half-tick is the proper time of the photon
claims: In the ship frame, E at the lower mirror and R at the upper mirror are vertically separated by 4 diagram units.
At 0.6c, during the same E to R interval the ship moves sideways 3 units in the Earth frame. The upper mirror is at the new position when R occurs.
The Earth path is 5 units and the ship path 4 units. Both assign the same speed to the light, so Earth assigns the longer time.
question: Why does the same pulse take longer between the same two events in Earth's frame?

transfer.question: Why is the Earth interval 5/4 of the ship interval in this drawing?
transfer.answer: Light covers five versus four units at the same speed.

stages: Show both labeled frames and trace E to R vertically in Ship; Earth starts at E.
Keep the reference diagram. In Earth show both mirrors' new positions and the horizontal displacement.
In Earth connect E to R at the new upper mirror and show 5 versus 4 units. Keep both frames visible.
editorial_direction: Open on two reunited twins with disagreeing working clocks. Both started together. Return to this exact mystery at the end. Earth times are synchronized coordinate measurements, not the light delay to one eye.

chapters.question: How can two good clocks disagree?
chapter_claims: Fictional reunion; both clocks ran normally and were together at departure and return.
Compare elapsed time, not a clock fault or light-travel delay.

reunion: The reunited twins compare two clocks that ran normally. One measured less time.
Ask how two working clocks disagree. Do not answer yet.
depart: At their common departure the clocks were synchronized. One twin stays on Earth and one travels.
The twin feels normal. No claims about seeing tick speeds during the trip in this chapter.

chapters.question: What makes a tick?
chapter_claims: A full tick is lower mirror to upper mirror and back.
Follow only emission E to reflection R, a half-tick; not the proper time of a photon.
stages: Use the straight four-unit path in the labeled ship frame.
Treat the moving mirror as a question before drawing the pulse.

chapters.question: Where does the upper mirror actually meet that pulse?
chapter_claims: In the ship frame, E at the lower mirror and R at the upper mirror are vertically separated by 4 diagram units.
At 0.6c, during the same E to R interval the ship moves sideways 3 units in the Earth frame. The upper mirror is at the new position when R occurs.
The Earth path is 5 units and the ship path 4 units. Both assign the same speed to the light, so Earth assigns the longer time.
stages: Show both labeled frames and trace E to R vertically in Ship; Earth starts at E.
Keep the reference diagram. In Earth show both mirrors' new positions and the horizontal displacement.

chapters.question: How large can that difference be?
chapter_claims: Switch from the diagram's 0.6c to a different constant-speed leg at 0.99c.
At 0.99c one ship year corresponds to about 7.09 Earth-frame years, not a whole round trip.
The traveler feels normal. Say the decimal in words.
stages: Show the ship year and new speed.
Emphasize that both clocks behave normally.

speed: This is a NEW demonstration: ninety-nine percent of the speed of light, not nine tenths.
Show a one year reading on the ship for this constant-speed leg. Earth number is still hidden.
one-year: Ninety-nine percent of light speed, exactly as shown. One year on ship; about seven point zero nine years of Earth-frame time.
compare-years: Both clocks work normally. The traveler does not feel slowed.
The example is for one constant-speed leg, not the full trip.

chapters.question: Why does the result not cancel at reunion?
chapter_claims: At turnaround the traveling twin changes inertial frames; the two worldlines between the same endpoint events differ.
The travelers' clocks record their own elapsed time. GPS accounts for motion and gravity; no numeric GPS claim.
Return to the meaning of the reunited clocks after GPS.
stages: Trace the two paths and common endpoints.
Brief application to satellite clock rates.
Pay off the question of the two clocks.

paths: Both worldlines start and end together. The traveler changes inertial frame at turnaround.
The elapsed proper time differs along the two paths. Do not infer elapsed time from drawn Euclidean line lengths.
gps: Motion AND weaker gravity affect GPS satellite clocks; the effects have opposite signs.
Do not say GPS orbiting clocks run slower overall. No drift numbers are required.
reunion: Return to the clocks: elapsed time is what each clock accumulated along its own path.
Neither clock malfunctioned; the two different readings are compatible.
